title: Chris Kelly's playing and where they worked
summary: Allen links the blues to Chris Kelly; Humphrey praises his style, tone and mutes and lists halls they played.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band

blocks.x: It sounds a bit like that blues that I believe Chris Kelly used to play.
That's Chris Kelly's band I was playing with then.

It used to be as funny as the good ones. Yeah. And with that thing that you were humming there, was that the trumpet part? Yeah, that's the starry blues. And I know that it was this blues that they recorded, and of course Chris Kelly never made any records either, but this record that they made in 1943 with Kit Howard. Supposed to have played a little bit like him.
Yeah. And he plays this careless love, and then before the careless love, they have this blues. Yeah. With the da-da-da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Well that's the same thing. Sounds like...
But he put the careless love, the only one in there. Right.
Yeah. Well, tell me something about Chris Kelly, because he's another one who's never recorded and so on. Oh, he's a swell trumpet bell, man. That line of...

He had a style of his own. Yes. Hard-working man. Wonderful tone. He was just a all around good jazz trumpet bell. Awesome. He didn't overdo nothing. Awesome. He used various kinds of mutes. Yeah. Whereabouts would you play with him? Oh, we played all over Louisiana. Different places, lots of fraternities and dances. Mm-hmm. All the halls down there. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. such as the Corporatees Hall, the Economy Hall, the New Hall, the outdoor lawn forties. That used to be a pretty great company. Besides, we did lots of work out in the Irish Channel, some up in the university, country clubs.
